summary: This unit teaches you to install electrical equipment correctly for Jamaican conditions and then to keep it working: switchboards, motor starters, control panels, pumps, fans, water heaters, lighting, emergency lighting, UPS units, batteries and standby generators. You will learn the types of maintenance and how to plan a programme, what is checked and tested, which work is done dead and which only the authorised person does live, how to deal with heat, damp, salt, pests and storms, and how to keep records and write a report the client can act on.

blocks.p: Electrical equipment fails for a few repeated reasons: joints work loose and overheat, insulation gets damp or dirty, bearings run dry, filters block, batteries age, and the environment gets inside. Most of these can be seen coming. At Level 3 you are expected to install equipment so that it starts life right, to plan the maintenance that keeps it right, to lead the team that does the work, to judge readings and trends, and to tell the client clearly what was found and what to do about it.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan an installation from the data
Read the drawings and the maker's data; check that the supply, the circuit, the isolator and the fixings suit the equipment and the place.
Install equipment correctly
Mount it level and secure, keep the maker's clearances, bring cables in through the right glands, earth and label it, and do the dead tests.
Hand it over
Record the tests and settings, give the client the manual and a maintenance schedule, and show them how to isolate it.
Choose the type of maintenance
Explain breakdown, planned preventive and condition-based maintenance, and say where each fits.
Build a maintenance programme
Make an asset register, rank the equipment, set tasks and intervals from the makers' manuals and local conditions, and plan shutdowns and spares.
Carry out maintenance safely
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead; barrier live parts; leave live checks to the authorised person.
Maintain the main types of equipment
Boards and starters, motors, batteries and UPS units, emergency lighting, generators, lighting and outdoor equipment.
Judge readings and trends
Compare readings with the maker's limits and with past readings, and act on a trend before it becomes a failure.
Supervise and record
Brief and check the team, keep records that show trends, and write a prioritised report.

blocks.note: As a trainee you work only on equipment that is **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead**, with the tester checked before and after. Live checks such as thermal imaging, running currents and the restoring of supply are done by the **authorised person**. Keep this split in mind in every section of this kit.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: The JPS supply is **50 Hz**, 110/220 V single-phase or three-phase at larger sites. Much equipment on sale in Jamaica is made for the US market, so check every nameplate for 50 Hz and for the right voltage. Heat, humidity, salt air, dust, pests, lightning and hurricanes all shorten the life of equipment here, and the maintenance intervals in a maker's manual are usually written for a milder climate.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Good maintenance starts with a good installation. Equipment that is mounted in the wrong place, fed from the wrong circuit or left without labels will keep the maintenance team busy for years.

head: Check
Against what
Why
rows: Voltage, phases and frequency
The nameplate against the supply
A 380–415 V three-phase machine cannot run on a 110/220 V single-phase supply; a 60 Hz-only motor runs slow and hot on 50 Hz.
Full-load current and starting current
The circuit, cable, breaker and isolator
The circuit must carry the running current and ride through the start.
Local isolator
Within sight of the equipment, lockable, out of reach of water
Anyone servicing it must be able to isolate it safely.
Protection
Overload set to the nameplate current; GFCI where the code requires it
Protects the motor and the people.
Mounting
The wall or floor, the weight, and fixings rated for that material
A 40 kg transformer on hollow block needs anchors made for hollow block, or through-bolts.
Clearances and cooling
The maker's figures
Drives, UPS units and transformers need air; service access needs space.
Enclosure rating
The location: indoors, outdoors, wind-driven rain, hose-down, salt
An IP or NEMA rating that suits the place.
Heat sources and fire
Kitchen extract fans, heaters, lamps near stored goods
Grease, dust and stored materials burn.

blocks.note: If the equipment and the supply do not match, **stop**. Do not try to 'make up' 220 V from two 110 V circuits, do not fit a bigger breaker and hope, and do not connect a 415 V machine to 220 V 'to see'. Advise the client on a suitable supply or another machine, in writing.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Mount enclosures **plumb and firm**. Use a spirit level, and check the wall for hidden cables and pipes with a detector before drilling.

Bring cables into outdoor enclosures **from below** through a gland of the right size for the cable, with its seal, so that water, dust and insects cannot follow the cable in. A top entry needs a sealing gland and a drip loop.
Close every unused knockout with a blanking plug.
Fit a **lockable local isolator**. A water heater's isolator in a bathroom goes out of reach of the shower spray, as the code and the maker say.
Earth every exposed metal part, and bond the door with a flexible strap where it carries devices.
Label the equipment, its isolator and its circuit at the board, so that anyone can identify it and isolate the right supply.

blocks.h: Example: an outdoor lighting control panel

flow: Check the lighting load against the contactor's rating for that kind of load (LED drivers draw a high inrush)
Choose an enclosure rated for wind-driven rain and salt air, with corrosion-resistant fixings
Mount it where it is reachable, above flood water and clear of vehicles
Place the photocell where it sees the sky but not the lights it controls
With the supply isolated and proved dead: glands from below, lockable isolator, numbered wiring, earth and labels
Dead tests: protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance, polarity
The authorised person energises, sets the time switch and checks the photocell and contactor
Hand over the drawing, settings, test results and a maintenance schedule

blocks.p: The client receives the **test results**, the **maker's operation and maintenance (O&M) manual**, the settings, the drawing or circuit chart, and a **maintenance schedule** that says what is done, how often, by whom and what is recorded. Show the client's staff how to isolate the equipment and what the alarms mean. Keep a copy of everything in your own records: it is the baseline for every later test.

sections.title: Types of maintenance and the maintenance programme

head: Type
What it is
Good for
Drawbacks
rows: **Breakdown** (corrective, reactive, run-to-failure)
Repair only after it fails.
Cheap, non-critical items whose failure is harmless: a lamp in a store room, a desk fan.
Failure comes without warning, often at the worst time, and can damage other things or stop the business.
**Planned preventive** (time-based)
Service at set intervals: by calendar or by running hours.
Items where failure matters and wear is predictable: pumps, emergency lights, generators, boards.
Some parts are replaced while they still had life in them; the work has to be planned round the business.
**Condition-based** (predictive)
Measure the condition (insulation resistance, vibration, temperature, running hours) and act when readings change.
Costly or critical items: large motors, main switchboards, transformers.
Needs instruments, skill and good records.

blocks.p: Most sites use a **mix**: breakdown maintenance for small things, planned preventive maintenance for the bulk of the equipment, and condition monitoring for the items that matter most.

flow: Survey the site and build the asset register
Collect the makers' manuals and any past records
Rank each item by how critical it is
Set the tasks and intervals from the manuals, adjusted for local conditions
Plan safe isolation, shutdowns at quiet times and the spares to hold
Write a checklist and a record sheet for each task
Do the work, record it, and review the programme every year against the records and the breakdowns

head: Tool
What it holds
rows: **Asset register**
Every item: its number, location, make and model, rating, date installed, and a link to its manual and history. It is the backbone of the programme: you cannot maintain what you do not know you have.
**Criticality ranking**
What happens if the item fails: danger to people, loss of business, cost of damage. A hotel's main switchboard, fire pump, water pumps and emergency lights come first; a store-room light comes last.
**Maintenance schedule**
For each item: the tasks, the interval, who does them (trainee, electrician, authorised person, maker's engineer) and what is recorded.
**Checklists and record sheets**
So the same checks are made every time, with real readings written down.
**CMMS** (computerised maintenance management system)
Software that holds the register, schedules the work, and keeps the records and trends. A spreadsheet and a logbook do the same for a small site.
**Critical spares list**
The parts that would otherwise stop the business for days: a pump's contactor and capacitor, a generator's starting battery, drive fans, breakers of unusual types.

ul: A motor's bearings are to be greased every **2,400 running hours**. It runs 12 hours a day, 6 days a week: 72 hours a week, so 2,400 ÷ 72 = about 33 weeks. The greasing goes on the schedule at about 8 months, and the running hours are checked on the hour meter.

A maker says 'inspect yearly'. On a coastal site with salt air and daily hose-down, the first year's findings may justify **every six months**. Set intervals from the manual, then shorten them where the records show that conditions are harsh.

A **planned shutdown** (outage) is agreed in advance with the client, at a quiet time, with everyone affected told. For a hotel's main switchboard that means a low-occupancy period, out of hours, with the generator or a temporary supply covering what must stay on.

blocks.h: When the plan is not working

blocks.p: If the same machine fails three times in a month, the plan is wrong for it. Ask **why**: loose connections (why do they loosen: vibration, heat, the wrong terminal?), damp, a worn part, misuse. Add a task that finds the cause earlier, shorten the interval, or change the installation. Keep records of breakdowns as carefully as records of planned work: the breakdowns are what improve the plan.

Energy = power × time. A 3 kW water heater running 5 hours a day for 30 days uses 3 × 5 × 30 = **450 kWh**. At a tariff the client gives you, say J$55 per kWh, that is 450 × 55 = **J$24,750** for the month, before GCT and the fixed charges on the bill. Figures like this help a client decide whether a timer, a thermostat setting, a cleaned heat exchanger or a new, efficient motor is worth paying for.

sections.title: Safe maintenance: dead work and live checks

flow: Read the manual and the last records; plan the tasks and who leads each
Agree the shutdown with the client, and get a permit if the site uses them
Write a short risk assessment for the job and the place
Isolate at the supply: switch off, lock off with a group hasp and each person's own padlock, and tag
Prove the tester on a proving unit, prove dead between every pair of conductors at the point of work, prove the tester again
Fit barriers or shrouds on any parts nearby that stay live, and mark them
Only now open covers and start work

head: Done dead, by the team
Done live, only by the authorised person
rows: Cleaning and inspection
Torque checks on terminals
Changing contacts, fuses, lamps and filters
Insulation resistance and continuity tests
Setting overloads and timers
Greasing bearings
Battery terminal checks, with the charger and load isolated as the maker says
Thermal imaging of boards on load
Measuring running currents and voltages
Pressing a GFCI's test button on a live circuit, and RCD trip-time tests
Reading drive fault logs on a running drive
Restoring the supply and checking operation
Generator test runs on load

blocks.note: A live reading is useful only when it is taken **before** the shutdown: a loose joint shows hot only while current flows through it. So the sequence is: live survey by the authorised person on load, then shutdown and dead work, then the authorised person restores the supply and checks.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Risk assessment: what to think about

head: Place
Hazards to list
rows: Roof space above a classroom or hotel corridor
Heat and dehydration, poor access, fragile ceiling boards, old cables, poor lighting, dust, wasps and rats.
Plant room or battery room
Hydrogen, acid, noise, hot surfaces, stored energy in capacitors and batteries, confined space.
Outdoors
Rain and wet ground, sun, ladders, overhead JPS lines, traffic, lizards and ants in panels.
Occupied buildings
People walking into the work area, children, equipment that others may switch on, noise and dust reaching guests or patients.

ul: **Capacitors** in motor starters, drives, UPS units and power factor banks hold a charge after isolation. Wait the time on the maker's label and check with a tester before touching.
**Batteries** cannot be switched off. Isolate the charger and the load, use insulated tools, and remove rings and watches.
**Springs** in breaker mechanisms and **pressure** in pneumatic parts are discharged as the maker says.
After an insulation resistance test, **discharge the circuit** before anyone touches it: the tester has charged it.

blocks.note: When only one section of a large switchboard can be isolated, the live sections beside it are the real danger. Fit shrouds or barriers, mark them 'LIVE', keep tools and leads away from them, and brief everyone before the covers come off.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Annual maintenance of a board or motor control centre

flow: Live survey on load by the authorised person: thermal image, running currents, any smell or noise
Shutdown: isolate, lock off, tag, prove dead; barrier live sections
Vacuum out dust (never blow it in with compressed air); clean insulators
Inspect for heat marks, discoloured terminals, corrosion, water marks, insects and damage
Check every terminal with a torque screwdriver to the maker's figure; record any that were loose
Inspect contactor contacts; check overload settings against each motor's nameplate
Insulation resistance of the motor circuits, with electronics disconnected
Remake any joint that showed hot on the thermal image
Dead tests after the work; covers on; locks off in order
Supply restored by the authorised person; operation checked; readings recorded and compared with last year's

head: Finding
Likely cause
Action
rows: A terminal shows hot on the thermal image
Loose connection, corroded conductor, under-sized cable or an overloaded circuit
Isolate; remake the joint; check the cable size and the load; retest.
Contactor contacts pitted and burnt
Normal arcing over time, made worse by chattering or an overloaded contactor
Replace the contacts or the contactor as the maker says. Never file them: filing removes the contact material and they fail faster.
Contactor hums or chatters
Low control voltage, dirt on the magnet faces, a weak coil, or a control transformer too small for the load
Clean the faces; check the control voltage under load; check the transformer's VA against the coils and lamps it feeds.
Control transformer very hot
Overloaded beyond its VA rating, or a shorted turn
Add up the load; replace or upsize.
Overload relay set above the motor's nameplate current
Someone 'stopped it tripping'
Set it to the nameplate current, as the maker says, and find out why it was tripping.
Ants, lizard nests, rat droppings, burn marks on a terminal
Open entries and gaps; warmth attracts them
Isolate, clean, repair the damage, seal unused entries and gaps, close the door properly.

blocks.note: **Torque, not strength.** A torque screwdriver set in newton metres (N·m) to the maker's figure tightens every terminal the same. Over-tightening strips threads, cracks terminals and crushes conductors; under-tightening leaves the joint to heat up. Both end in a burnt terminal.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: The user presses the **test button** at the interval on the maker's label (often monthly). The device must trip at once. One that does not is reported and replaced.
The authorised person tests trip time with an RCD tester during periodic testing.
A device that trips now and then with no fault may be seeing the small leakage currents of many electronic loads added together; the circuits are split over more devices.

head: Task
Points to watch
rows: Bearings

Grease with the **type and amount** the maker gives, at the interval in running hours. Too much grease churns, overheats the bearing and can be forced into the windings. Sealed-for-life bearings are not greased: they are replaced.
Cooling
Clean the fan cover and fins. A motor caked in dust, grease or feathers runs hot, and heat is what ages insulation.
Insulation resistance
Tested at the same voltage and, as far as possible, the same temperature each time, with the motor disconnected from its drive or starter. Compare with the previous readings.
Terminal box
Tight connections, sound gland, no water, no corrosion.
Vibration and noise
A change points to bearings, misalignment, a loose foot or an unbalanced fan.
Running current
Measured by the authorised person; compared with the nameplate and past readings.

blocks.p: Readings taken once a year in the same conditions: **250 MΩ, 240 MΩ, 80 MΩ, 10 MΩ**. The first two are high and steady: healthy. Then the reading falls sharply, twice. Even if 10 MΩ is still above the minimum in the specification, the **trend** says the insulation is deteriorating, probably from moisture, dirt, oil or heat, and that the next reading may be a failure. The right response is to plan the work now: isolate, inspect the terminal box, gland and windings, clean and dry by an approved method, retest, and if the reading does not recover, plan a rewind or replacement at a convenient time. Test more often until the trend is steady again. Waiting for it to fail means an unplanned stoppage, usually at the busiest moment.

blocks.note: An insulation reading on its own tells you less than a reading **compared with the last one**. That is why every test is recorded with its date, instrument, test voltage and the conditions.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Batteries, UPS units and standby generators

head: Hazard
Why
Precaution
rows: **Hydrogen gas**
Given off during charging, especially by vented (flooded) cells; it explodes from a spark or flame.
A ventilated room, no smoking or flames, no sparks: isolate the charger and the load before disconnecting anything.
**Short circuit**
A battery cannot be switched off. A spanner across the terminals causes a flash, burns and molten metal.
Insulated tools, one connection at a time, remove rings and watches, cover terminals not being worked on.
**Acid**
Corrosive to skin and eyes; burns clothing.
Goggles or a face shield, acid-resistant gloves and apron; an eyewash station and water close by; neutraliser for spills, as the safety data sheet says.
**Weight**
Cells and blocks are heavy and awkward.
Lift with help or a trolley; keep feet clear.
**Heat**
Battery life falls sharply as temperature rises: roughly halved for every 8 to 10 °C above the maker's design temperature (commonly 20 to 25 °C).
A cool room, clearances for air, no direct sun on the cabinet.

ul: Capacity is given in **ampere-hours (Ah)**. Ignoring losses, a 12 V, 150 Ah battery can supply 15 A for about 150 ÷ 15 = **10 hours**. In practice, a heavy load, age and heat all reduce this, and deep discharges shorten battery life.
**Sealed (valve-regulated, VRLA)** batteries need no topping up and give off little gas in normal use, but they still vent if overcharged or hot, so the room is ventilated as the maker says.
**Vented (flooded)** batteries need topping up with distilled or deionised water, electrolyte checks and more ventilation.
Old batteries go to an **approved recycler**. Lead and acid must never go into the general waste, the ground or a drain.

head: Installation
Maintenance
rows: A dry, cool, ventilated room with the maker's clearances
A floor that can carry the batteries' weight
Supply cable and protection sized from the maker's data, with a lockable isolator
A bypass switch, so the UPS can be serviced without losing the supply
Output circuits clearly labelled, so staff know what is on the UPS
Earthing as the maker's manual says
Commissioned by the authorised person, including a run-time test on battery
Check the display and alarms, and the event log
Keep the room within the maker's temperature range; clean filters and fans
Check battery terminals for corrosion and tightness, with the system isolated as the maker says
Periodic battery tests; replace batteries at the end of their life (often 3 to 5 years for sealed types in warm rooms)
Keep records of every check and every battery date

blocks.note: A UPS protects what is plugged into its **output**. If a hospital's or clinic's staff plug the critical equipment into an ordinary outlet, the UPS does nothing for them. Clear labels on the UPS outlets are part of the installation.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A generator that has not run for months may not start when the lights go out. The authorised person runs it **at set intervals, on load**, to prove that it starts, takes the load and holds voltage and 50 Hz. A short run off load does not prove much and lets unburnt fuel build up in the exhaust.
Routine checks: starting battery and charger, fuel level and condition, coolant, oil, belts, exhaust, leaks, the transfer switch and the alarms, and the running hours.
The fuel in a tank that is rarely used goes stale and grows algae in Jamaica's heat; plan fuel checks and treatment.
Only a proper **transfer switch** connects a generator. A generator connected without one can feed back into the JPS lines and kill a line worker.

sections.title: Emergency lighting, lighting and outdoor equipment

head: Test
How often (typical)
What it proves
rows: Short function test
Monthly

Each fitting switches to its battery (often with a test key switch or test button) and lights, then returns to normal and shows its charging indicator. Proves the lamp, the battery and the changeover.
**Full-duration test**
Yearly, or as the specification says
The fittings run on battery for their **full rated time** (commonly 1 to 3 hours). Proves the batteries still hold enough charge to light the escape routes for as long as is required.

ul: The full-duration test is done at a **quiet time**, because the batteries take many hours to recharge and the building is less protected until they do. In a hotel that means a low-occupancy daytime, never the evening before a full house.
Clean lenses and diffusers; replace failed lamps and batteries promptly; a fitting that goes out early in the test fails the test.
Record every test in a **logbook**. The fire authority, the insurer and the building's owner may ask to see it.
Emergency lighting is a life-safety system. A fitting that goes out after ten minutes is not a snag to clear later: it is fixed before the building is relied on.

Dust and dirt on fittings cut the light reaching the floor badly over time, so fittings are cleaned as a group at set intervals, not one at a time when someone complains. A warehouse with 120 high-bay fittings is cleaned on a planned cycle from a mobile platform.
LED fittings last long, but their **drivers** fail from heat. Check the driver's maximum working temperature against the ceiling space it is in.
LED lamps on an old dimmer flicker or buzz when the dimmer is not compatible with them. Fit a dimmer made for LED loads.

blocks.h: Jamaican conditions: what to look for and what to do

head: Condition
What it does
Install and maintain
rows: Heat
Shortens the life of batteries, capacitors, drives and electronics; overheats motors
Ventilation and clearances; shade; temperature checks during maintenance; shorter battery life allowed for.
Humidity and rain
Moisture in enclosures and motors; tracking and corrosion
The right IP rating, glands from below, seals and gaskets, anti-condensation heaters; regular insulation resistance tests.
Salt air on the coast
Fast corrosion of metal parts, joints and fixings
Corrosion-resistant enclosures and fixings; protected joints; inspection more often.
Sun (ultraviolet)
Cracks PVC cable sheaths and plastic enclosures
Sun-resistant (UV-rated) cable, or cable protected in conduit; replace cracked, brittle cable; never paint, tape or oil it.
Dust from roads, quarries and sugar factories
Blocks filters and fans; dust and damp track across terminals
Filters that can be cleaned; a cleaning schedule; vacuum, never blow.
Pests: ants, lizards, wasps, rats
Nests, chewed insulation, short circuits, burnt terminals
Blanking plugs and glands on every entry; no gaps; doors kept shut; clean and inspect; never spray insecticide into a live panel.
Lightning and switching surges
Damaged electronics, drivers and controls
Surge protection and sound earthing; check SPD indicators after storms.
Hurricanes and floods
Wind damage; water in equipment
Mount above known flood level; anchor firmly; after a storm, inspect, dry and test before re-energising; never switch on flooded equipment.
Kitchen grease
Coats extract fan motors, blocks cooling and is a fire risk
Clean the fan and ducts on a schedule; check the motor's temperature and current.

blocks.note: Equipment that has been under flood water is not switched on 'to see'. Water leaves silt and salt inside breakers, contactors and windings. It is isolated, opened, cleaned, dried and tested, and often the devices are replaced, before the authorised person re-energises it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Records, reports and supervising the team

ul: They **prove the work was done**: for the client, the insurer, the fire authority and, after an accident, the investigators.
They **show trends**: insulation falling, current rising, a contactor replaced every six months.
They **give a baseline** for the next test and for a new electrician who has never seen the site.
They hold the **settings**: overloads, timers, drive parameters, time switch programmes, so that a replacement can be set up correctly.

blocks.p: Every task is recorded with the **date**, the **equipment number**, the **readings** (not just 'OK'), the **instrument** used, what was **found** and **done**, and the **name** of the person who did it.

head: Part
What it contains
rows: Heading
Site, date, who did the work, what was checked.
Findings
For each item: what was checked, the readings, pass or fail, with photographs.
Problems in priority order
**Urgent**: dangerous now (a missing earth, a damaged cable, a burnt terminal). Made safe on the day and reported straight away.
**Soon**: will fail or become unsafe (worn contacts, a falling insulation trend, a weak generator battery).
**Watch**: in order, but changing; test again at the next visit.
Recommended actions
What to do, by when, and an estimated cost in J$, with GCT at the current rate where it applies.
Sign-off
Who did the work and who received the report.

blocks.p: Go through the report with the owner in plain words, answer questions, agree what will be done and when, and file a copy. A report that sits in a drawer unread has not done its job; one that frightens the owner with jargon has not either.

ul: Give each task a **checklist** and a record sheet, so that nothing is skipped and the readings are written down as they are taken.
**Show the first ones**, then let the trainee do the next under your eye, then **spot-check** a sample of the rest. Signing off thirty emergency lights together at the end of the day is not a check.
Never let a trainee take live readings or restore a supply. Make the split between dead work and the authorised person's work clear at the briefing.
Check that every member's padlock is on the hasp before covers come off, and that nobody removes another person's lock.
Look at the trainee's records as well as the work: a reading written as 'OK' is sent back.
Lead-acid batteries to an approved recycler; never the skip, the ground or a drain.
Fluorescent tubes and some lamps contain mercury: handled and disposed of as the Centre's or the client's procedure says.
Old oil, grease and contaminated rags are kept apart from general waste.
Scrap copper and steel are recycled; records of what was removed stop disputes.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can check a new item of equipment against the supply, the circuit, the isolator, the fixings and the place before it is installed.
I can describe a correct installation: mounting, glands from below, lockable isolator, earthing, labels and dead tests.
I can say what is handed over with new equipment.
I can explain breakdown, planned preventive and condition-based maintenance and give an example of each.
I can build an asset register, rank equipment by criticality, and set tasks and intervals from the manual and local conditions.
I can work out an interval in weeks from running hours, and the cost of running a load in J$.
I can isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead, and say which checks only the authorised person does live.
I can list the annual tasks on a switchboard and starter and say what a hot joint, pitted contacts and a chattering contactor mean.
I can explain why terminals are torqued, not tightened as hard as possible.
I can grease a motor bearing correctly and read an insulation resistance trend.
I can list the hazards of lead-acid batteries and the precautions, and work out a battery's run time.
I can say what a UPS installation needs and what its maintenance plan includes.
I can explain the monthly and full-duration tests of emergency lighting and when to do the full test.
I can say why a generator is run on load and why a transfer switch is essential.
I can say how heat, humidity, salt, sun, dust, pests, lightning and floods affect equipment and what to do about each.
I can record a task properly and write a report sorted by priority.
I can supervise trainees on routine checks with checklists, demonstration and spot-checks.

head: Figure or formula
What it is
rows: Weeks = running hours interval ÷ running hours per week
Turning a maker's hours interval into a schedule
Hours = Ah ÷ A
A battery's run time, ignoring losses
kWh = kW × hours; cost = kWh × tariff
The cost of running a load
I = VA ÷ V
The current a control transformer can supply
N·m (newton metres)
The unit a torque screwdriver is set in
Monthly; yearly
Typical short and full-duration emergency lighting tests
About halved per 8 to 10 °C above design temperature
How battery life falls with heat
50 Hz
The JPS supply frequency

terms: Asset register
The list of all the equipment a team looks after, with its location, details and history.
Authorised person
The competent person appointed to do live checks, switching and energising.
Breakdown maintenance
Repair done only after equipment has failed; also called corrective or reactive maintenance, or run-to-failure.
CMMS
Computerised maintenance management system: software that schedules maintenance and keeps its records.
Condition-based maintenance
Measuring the condition of equipment and acting when the readings change.
Critical spares
Parts kept in stock because a breakdown without them would stop the business for days.
Full-duration test
Running emergency lights on battery for their full rated time.
Hydrogen
The explosive gas given off by lead-acid batteries during charging.
Insulation resistance trend
A series of readings taken in the same conditions over time; a fall shows deterioration before failure.
O&M manual
The maker's operation and maintenance manual.
Pitting
The small craters burnt into contactor contacts by arcing.
Planned preventive maintenance
Servicing at set intervals, by calendar or running hours, to stop failures.
Shutdown (planned outage)
A stop of equipment agreed in advance so that maintenance can be done.
Snag list
The list of faults found during an inspection or installation that must be put right.
Thermal imaging
Using an infrared camera on a board under load to find joints running hot.
Torque screwdriver
A screwdriver set in newton metres that tightens every terminal to the maker's figure.
Transfer switch
The switch that moves a building's load between the mains and a generator and never connects both together.
UPS
Uninterruptible power supply: keeps equipment running from a battery when the mains fails.
Vented and sealed batteries
Flooded lead-acid cells that need topping up, and valve-regulated cells that do not.

c1.title: A maintenance programme for a Runaway Bay resort
c1.text: Natalie, a Level 3 electrician, has been asked to set up planned maintenance for a 90-room beachfront resort in Runaway Bay, St Ann. The resort has a main switchboard, a standby generator, three water pumps, a fire pump, 60 emergency lights, a kitchen with two extract fans, and a laundry. The resort keeps no records and no list of its equipment. The maker's manual for the water pump motors says 'inspect annually' and 'grease bearings every 2,400 running hours'; the pumps run 12 hours a day, 7 days a week. The resort is full from December to April.

c2.title: Annual shutdown at a Linstead juice factory
c2.text: Dwayne, a Level 3 electrician, leads the annual maintenance of the motor control centre at a juice factory in Linstead, St Catherine. Before the shutdown, the authorised person's thermal image shows the outgoing terminal of the crusher starter at 74 °C while similar terminals read 36 °C. The crusher motor's nameplate current is 28 A; its overload relay is found set at 36 A, and a maintenance worker says he raised it 'because it kept tripping'. The main contactor of the bottling line has deeply pitted contacts, and the 220/24 V control transformer is too hot to touch.

c3.title: A UPS for a Black River pharmacy
c3.text: A pharmacy in Black River, St Elizabeth, is installing a 3 kVA UPS with a cabinet of sealed lead-acid batteries to keep its dispensing computers, fridge alarms and point-of-sale terminals running through outages. The owner wants it in a small store room with no window that stays at about 34 °C in the afternoon. The batteries are 12 V, 100 Ah; the critical load on battery is about 20 A at 12 V equivalent. Kemisha, a Level 3 electrician, is planning the installation and the maintenance.

c4.title: An outdoor pump panel at a Hopewell fish farm
c4.text: At a fish farm in Hopewell, Hanover, two aerator pumps are fed from an outdoor panel beside the ponds, 300 m from the sea. The PVC cable to one pump has cracked and gone brittle in the sun. Inside the panel Jerome, a Level 3 electrician, finds a wasp nest, ant trails to a terminal with burn marks, and water stains below the top cable entry. The panel's old photocell switches the pond lights, and the 20 A breaker feeding the lights trips about once a week.

c5.title: Emergency lights at a Port Antonio hospital wing
c5.text: Simone, a Level 3 electrician, supervises two trainees on the emergency lighting of a hospital wing in Port Antonio, Portland: 48 fittings, each rated for 3 hours on battery. The wing is busiest in the evening. In last month's test two fittings went out after about 20 minutes, and one shows no charging indicator. The trainees want to finish the 48 fittings quickly and sign the logbook together at the end.

questions.q: What should Natalie do first?
o: Order a year's spares for every item on the resort
Start a schedule from the maker's manual for the pumps
Survey the resort and build an asset register of its equipment
Book the first shutdown of the main switchboard for next week
questions.why: You cannot plan maintenance for equipment you have not listed. The register records each item, its location, rating, age and manual, and is the base for ranking, scheduling, spares and records. Everything else follows from it.

questions.q: Which items should rank highest in Natalie's criticality list?
o: The main switchboard, fire pump, water pumps and emergency lights
The laundry machines, since they run for the most hours
The store-room and corridor lights, since there are most of them
The kitchen extract fans, since they are cleaned most often
questions.why: Criticality is about what happens when the item fails: danger to life (fire pump, emergency lights), loss of the whole business (main switchboard) and loss of guest service (water). Hours run and numbers of items do not decide it.

questions.q: About how often do the pump motors need greasing?
o: About every 7 weeks
About every 20 weeks
About every 29 weeks
About every 50 weeks
questions.why: The pumps run 12 × 7 = 84 hours a week, so 2,400 ÷ 84 = about 28.6 weeks. Read the hour meter at each visit rather than relying on the calendar, and use the type and amount of grease the maker gives.

questions.q: When should the main switchboard shutdown be planned, and why?
o: In January, when the generator can carry the whole resort
During the low season, out of hours, with staff and guests told
On a Saturday afternoon, when the most staff are on duty
Without notice at night, so that no guest has time to worry
questions.why: A shutdown is agreed in advance at a quiet time: the low season and out of hours, with everyone affected warned and cover arranged for what must stay on. The resort is full in January, and surprises are not acceptable in an occupied building.

questions.q: Should the 'inspect annually' interval for the pumps stay as it is?
o: Yes: a maker's interval may not be changed by the installer
Yes: a longer interval would be safe on a resort that is quiet in summer
No: in salt air and heat, a shorter interval is likely to be justified
No: pumps on a resort should be inspected every week
questions.why: A maker's interval is the starting point, usually written for a milder climate. Salt air, humidity and long running hours speed up corrosion and insulation damage, so the first year's findings will probably justify six-monthly inspection. The records decide.

questions.q: What does the 74 °C terminal most likely show, and what is done about it?
o: A loose or corroded joint: remake it during the dead work
The crusher is simply a heavy load: nothing is needed
A faulty thermal camera: take the image again later
A short circuit in the motor: replace the motor at once
questions.why: A joint 38 °C hotter than its neighbours on the same load is a high-resistance connection, usually loose or corroded. It is remade with the board isolated and proved dead, the cable and load are checked, and the authorised person scans it again when the supply is restored.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do about the overload relay set at 36 A?
o: Leave it, since the crusher clearly needs the extra current
Set it to 28 A and find out why the crusher was tripping it
Set it to 56 A, twice the nameplate, to stop nuisance trips
Remove the overload relay and rely on the circuit breaker
questions.why: The overload is set to the motor's nameplate current unless the maker says otherwise. At 36 A the motor could run at 130% of its rating and burn out. The tripping was a symptom: a jammed crusher, a low voltage, a hot motor or a bad joint, and the cause must be found.

questions.q: What is the right action for the deeply pitted contacts on the bottling line's contactor?
o: File them flat and smooth so that they close fully
Bend the contact carriers so that the contacts press harder
Replace the contacts or the contactor as the maker says
Coat them with contact grease so that they stop arcing
questions.why: Contacts are made of a special alloy, and their thickness is their life. Filing removes the alloy and leaves a rough surface that arcs more and welds. Bending or greasing does not restore the contact material. Replacement contacts, or a new contactor, is the only sound repair.

questions.q: The 220/24 V control transformer is too hot to touch. What is the first thing to check?
o: Whether the supply has changed from 50 Hz to 60 Hz
Whether the transformer case was painted a dark colour
Whether the 24 V side has too few loads connected
Whether the VA of the coils and lamps exceeds its rating
questions.why: A control transformer loaded beyond its VA rating overheats and its voltage sags, which also makes contactors chatter. Add up the VA of everything on together, allow for inrush, and replace it with a larger one if needed. A shorted turn is the other possibility.

questions.q: Why is the 34 °C store room a poor place for the battery cabinet?
o: High temperature shortens battery life sharply
Sealed batteries cannot charge above 30 °C
The UPS display cannot be read in the dark
The room is too warm for the pharmacy's fridges
questions.why: Battery life falls roughly by half for every 8 to 10 °C above the maker's design temperature, commonly 20 to 25 °C. In a 34 °C room the batteries may last less than half their rated life. Kemisha should propose a cooler, ventilated location or cooling for that room.

questions.q: Kemisha works out a run time of 5 hours from the batteries' ratings. Why should she warn the owner that the real figure may be shorter?
o: Batteries give their full rating only when charged from a generator
The UPS keeps most of the stored charge for its own display and fans
Ampere-hours are quoted for one 12 V battery, not for the whole cabinet
Heat, age and the UPS's own losses all reduce the usable capacity
questions.why: A rated capacity assumes new batteries at the maker's design temperature. In a 34 °C room, with ageing and the UPS's own losses, less is available. The authorised person measures the real run time at commissioning and records it as the baseline.

questions.q: Which feature lets the UPS be serviced later without cutting the supply to the pharmacy's computers?
o: A larger battery cabinet, so that the run time is longer
A second set of outlets fed straight from the board
A maintenance bypass switch in the installation
A lockable isolator fitted on the UPS's input
questions.why: A bypass switch puts the load straight onto the mains while the UPS is isolated for service or battery replacement. Outlets fed straight from the board would simply be unprotected, and the input isolator alone would cut the output.

questions.q: What should Kemisha's maintenance plan say about the battery terminals?
o: Check them while the UPS is running, so that the load is not disturbed
Check them with the system isolated, using insulated tools
Leave them alone, since sealed batteries never need any attention
Tighten them as hard as possible once a year with a long spanner
questions.why: A battery cannot be switched off, so a spanner across its terminals causes a flash and burns. The charger and load are isolated as the maker says, insulated tools are used, rings and watches come off, and terminals are checked for corrosion and tightness to the maker's torque.

questions.q: Why did the PVC sheath of the pump cable crack and go brittle?
o: Ultraviolet light in sunlight broke the plastic down over the years
The cable was pulled too tight when it was first run to the pump
The pump's motor sends too high a voltage along the cable
Rain soaked into the sheath, which makes PVC harden and split
questions.why: Sunlight's ultraviolet rays break down ordinary PVC, which then cracks right through. The damage cannot be repaired with tape, paint or oil. The lasting cure is sun-resistant (UV-rated) cable, or cable protected in conduit out of the sun.

questions.q: After the panel has been isolated and cleaned out, what stops the pests and the water coming back?
o: Spraying insecticide inside the panel each week while it is live
Leaving the door ajar so that the heat and insects can escape
Filling the inside of the panel with expanding foam to block gaps
Sealing every unused entry and gap, and entering from below
questions.why: Pests and water come in through open entries, gaps and a top cable entry. Blanking plugs, glands on every cable, sound gaskets, bottom entry with a drip loop, and a door kept shut are the lasting fixes. Insecticide in a live panel is a fire and shock hazard, and foam traps heat.

questions.q: The 20 A breaker feeding the pond lights trips about once a week. What should Jerome do?
o: Fit a 30 A breaker, so that the lights stay on through the night
Tape the breaker handle in the ON position until the season ends
Replace the breaker with a fuse, which will not trip as easily
Find the cause: the load, the wiring and the cable insulation
questions.why: A breaker that trips is protecting something. The lights and their inrush may overload the circuit, the sun-damaged cable may be leaking, or the photocell may be cycling. A larger device would let the cable overheat; defeating the breaker risks a fire.

questions.q: When should the full three-hour duration test of the wing's emergency lighting be done?
o: In the evening, when the wing is busiest and the staff can watch it
Just before a fire drill, so that both are over in one day
At night with the normal lights off, so that the fittings can be seen
On a quiet morning, so the batteries recharge before night
questions.why: After a full-duration test the batteries need many hours to recharge, and until they do the wing has little emergency lighting. The test is done at a quiet time, early enough for the fittings to be fully charged again before the busy evening and the night.

questions.q: What does a fitting that went out after 20 minutes of a 3-hour test tell Simone?
o: Its lamp is the wrong type and should be changed for a brighter one
Its battery no longer holds its charge: fix it before the wing relies on it
It is normal for some fittings to go out early in a long test
The test key switch is faulty, so the fitting should be retested next month
questions.why: The fitting did switch to its battery, so the lamp and changeover work; the battery has lost its capacity. Emergency lighting is a life-safety system, so the battery is replaced promptly and the fitting retested, not noted for later.

questions.q: How should Simone run the trainees' monthly checks on the 48 fittings?
o: Give them a checklist, show them the first few, and spot-check their work
Do all 48 fittings herself while the trainees watch and hold the ladder
Let them finish all 48 and sign the logbook together at the end of the day
Ask the ward staff to say which fittings looked dim and check only those
questions.why: A checklist makes every check the same; demonstrating sets the standard; recording each fitting as it is tested gives a true log; and spot-checks catch what was missed. Signing 48 fittings together at the end is not a record of anything.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW pump runs 8 hours a day for 30 days. The client's tariff is J$50 per kWh. About what does the pump cost to run for the month, before GCT and fixed charges?
questions.why: Energy = 1.5 kW × 8 h × 30 = 360 kWh. Cost = 360 × 50 = J$18,000. Working out the running cost shows the client what a timer, a smaller pump or a cleaned filter would save.
